summary:
Napas Gambut (Peat's Breath) is a web app in English and Bahasa Indonesia that tracks tropical peat drying using NISAR's L-band radar, which passes every 12 days. Team Betelgeuse built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge "Dancing with the SARs". It divides a study area in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, into 500 m cells

For each radar pass, it labels every cell as stable, drying, deep drying, re-wetting, on fire or burned. A cell gets a label only when its HH backscatter change is larger than the natural "wobble" (the noise floor) of dense forest on mineral soil, which is used as the reference.

This matters because drained peat dries out and then burns below the surface. Indonesia's 2015 fires cost US$16.1 billion. About a third of the burned area was peat, and peat fires made most of the haze. Restoration staff and village fire brigades must decide which canals to block before the next dry spell. Smoke and cloud block optical satellites at exactly the time they most need to see. L-band radar sees through haze, so the app keeps working when optical images fail, and it ranks which canals to block first.


The live app currently shows a clearly labelled simulated season. Real NISAR data replaces it without code changes.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Python pipeline:

  • Streams NISAR L2 GCOV radar data (HH/HV) from ASF and builds a 500 m grid from OSM canals, GFW peat and concession maps, and ESA WorldCover.
  • For each cell it computes a wetness index: the HH change since the first pass, minus the same change in the reference forest.
  • The noise floor σ is 1.4826 × MAD (median absolute deviation) of the reference forest's values.

Cell rules which is checked in order:

  1. No data
  2. Fire, radar agrees
  3. Fire, radar silent
  4. Burned
  5. Re-wetting
  6. Deep drying (more than 4σ)
  7. Drying (more than 2σ)
  8. Stable

Extra data joined in: NASA FIRMS fire detections, ERA5 rainfall, and cross-checks against SME2, MODIS burned area and Sentinel.

Static React + MapLibre app with five screens:

  • Smoke and radar: a swipe between a smoky image and the radar view of the same day.
  • Season map: plays every 12-day pass, with a pulse card per cell.
  • Scorecard: results by land type, canal-blocking priorities, dams to inspect, and self-checks.
  • Method: the method in plain language, its limits, and how AI was used.
  • Global peat: the world's large tropical peatlands that NISAR covers.

2. What benefit does it have?

  • Shows where peat is drying even when smoke and cloud blind optical satellites.
  • Gives restoration teams a ranked list of the top 20 drainage canals to block, plus dams to inspect.
  • Flags "fire, radar silent" cells, where fires were detected but the radar showed no sign. These are often low-intensity ground fires.
  • Needs no backend, works offline after the first visit, and is bilingual, which suits field teams with poor connectivity.

3. What is the intended impact?

We made this to help peat-restoration staff and village fire brigades decide where to block canals before the next dry spell, so fewer peat fires start and less haze is produced.

Planned future work:

  • A 12-day watch through each dry season, sent to restoration teams while there's still time to close canals.
  • A full-year record, to compare the dry season with the wet season that refills the peat.
  • The same method for the Congo Basin and the Peruvian Amazon.
  • Pairing NISAR's L-band with its S-band radar.

4. What tools, languages, and software were used?

  • Languages: Python 3.11+, Typescript.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Zod, d3-scale, d3-shape, Vitest, service worker for offline use.
  • Pipeline(data handling): NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, Xarray, Zarr, h5py.
  • Pipeline(maps and geometry): Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj, osmium
  • Pipeline(NASA and ASF access): asf_search, earthaccess
  • Machine Learning: scikit-learn (gradient-boosted trees, logistic regression), MAPIE conformal sets, cleanlab
  • Hosting: Cloudflare

AI coding assistants helped with the software and the Indonesian text. This is disclosed in the README and on the Method screen.

5. How is your project creative?

What we made is a system with these workflow:

Comparing each pass against a reference forest sets its own noise floor, meaning a cell is only labeled when the change rises clearly above that background noise.

When the radar does miss something, a dedicated "fire, radar silent" state, shown as a hollow ring, is upfront about those blind spots, while a simple smoke-versus-radar swipe lets you see NISAR's advantage in a single gesture.

To make the underlying science approachable, the Method screen relies on everyday metaphors, radar works "like a bat," with HH sensing the "floor" (soil and water) and HV picking up the "furniture" (leaves and branches). That same commitment to honesty carries into the modeling, where conformal sets allow the land-cover model to candidly say "radar can't tell" when uncertainty is high, and the fire-risk hindcast is only displayed if it actually beats simple baseline rules.

6.What factors did we consider?

  • Scientific limits: the index is a relative wetness signal, not water-table depth, dense canopy hides the peat surface, smouldering fires can leave the canopy standing, so the radar may stay silent, a 12-day gap can miss short fires.
  • Data honesty: a "Simulated data" badge on every screen the export refuses unverified radar data unless a flag explicitly allows it, model inputs avoid circular reasoning (canal density and drying are not land-cover inputs).
  • Real-world constraints: the NISAR provisional-data pause from 23 Oct to 6 Nov 2026, and no canal-block dam points found for the study area.
  • Accessibility: keyboard navigation, reduced motion, mobile layout, light and dark themes, two languages, and offline use.
  • Licences and attribution for every dataset.
